title: AgentRewardBench: Evaluating Automatic Evaluations of Web Agent Trajectories
authors: Lù, Kazemnejad, Meade, Patel et al.
takeaway: Benchmarks how well LLM judges assess web agent trajectories, across 1302 expert-annotated trajectories from 5 benchmarks and 4 LLMs. Two findings stand out: no single judge wins across all benchmarks, and rule-based evaluation systematically underreports agent success.

title: Corrective Retrieval Augmented Generation
takeaway: CRAG adds a lightweight retrieval evaluator that grades retrieved documents and triggers a different action depending on the verdict, falling back to web search when the retrieval looks wrong. The decompose-then-recompose step for stripping irrelevant passages is the part worth borrowing.

title: Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
takeaway: Trains a single model to decide when to retrieve and to critique its own output using reflection tokens, rather than retrieving on every query. Reads naturally alongside CRAG as the other answer to the same question: what to do when retrieval is the weak link.

title: Scalable AI Safety via Doubly-Efficient Debate
takeaway: Extends debate-based oversight to stochastic AI systems, with protocols where an honest debater wins using only polynomially many simulation steps even against a dishonest one allowed exponentially many. A complexity-theoretic take on scalable oversight rather than an empirical one.

title: Attention Is All You Need
takeaway: The paper that replaced recurrence with self-attention. Worth reading closely for how the scaled dot-product and multi-head formulation fall out of very simple linear algebra.

title: On the Difficulty of Training Recurrent Neural Networks
takeaway: Diagnoses vanishing and exploding gradients from analytical, geometric, and dynamical-systems angles, then proposes gradient norm clipping. Clipping is still standard practice in every training loop I write, which makes the original argument worth reading rather than inheriting.

title: A Neural Probabilistic Language Model
takeaway: The paper that introduced learned word embeddings, tackling the curse of dimensionality by having a neural net learn a distributed representation for words alongside the probability function. Every modern embedding traces back to this.
